new_statements.quote: 2.3.2 Word-stress. Each phonological word has a distinctive stress pattern in that its initial syllable is raised in pitch and is thereby prominent. The initial syllable bears primary stress, shown by [ˈ], e.g. ngutj [ˈŋuc] 'spirit'; punya [ˈpuɲæ] 'salmon'; ... Every third (odd-numbered) syllable thereafter carries secondary stress, shown by [ˌ], e.g. padjarranba [ˈpaɟaˌranba] 'parrotfish'; demiwulytjiwulytji [ˈdemɪwuˌʎcɪwuˌʎci] 'kidneys'. The final syllable of a polysyllabic word is unstressed ... Enclitic particles never bear stress, whether they occur word-finally ... or precede other enclitics" (Ford 1998:70). Bridge: "While Emmi and Mendhe share identical sound systems and grammar, they differ slightly in lexicon and morphology." (Marett, Barwick & Ford 2013:77-78)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Ford 1998 (ANU thesis, hdl 1885/10796), I rendered PDF p.94 (printed p.70) and read it. The section is headed '2.3.2 Word-stress' and reads exactly as quoted: 'Each phonological word has a distinctive stress pattern in that its initial syllable is raised in pitch and is thereby prominent. The initial syllable bears primary stress, shown by ['], e.g. ngutj.. punya.. ngupelh.. Every third (odd-numbered) syllable thereafter carries secondary stress.. padjarranba ['paɟaˌranba] 'parrotfish'; demiwulytjiwulytji.. 'kidneys'. The final syllable of a polysyllabic word is unstressed, e.g. ngammama.. pitjawakatj.. menbiya+rtedi.. Enclitic particles never bear stress, w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (realised as raised pitch) falls on the first syllable of every phonological word; the statement is made for Emmi, whose sound system Ford (2013) states is identical to that of its sister dialect Mendhe (= Manda/Menhthe).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables after the first (3rd, 5th..), but never on the final syllable of a polysyllabic word; coverbs, incorporated nominals and bound number words inside the verb complex carry secondary stress on their own initial syllable (Ford 1998:70-74, p.3).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitic particles and affixes are never stressed; final syllable of a polysyllable is unstressed even if odd-numbered; in serial constructions the second inflected verb loses primary stress and takes secondary stress (Ford 1998:70-75).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (which may be larger than the grammatical word: verb complex with coverbs/incorporated nominals shares one primary stress). Statement is for Emmi (amii1238); applied to Manda/Menhdhe only via Ford's explicit claim (2013:77-78) that Emmi and Mendhe have identical sound systems; no Menhdhe-specific stress data exist in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Ford 1998:70) describes Emmi (glottocode amii1238), not Manda/Menhthe itself. Ford treats 'Emmi and Menhdhe' as 'closely related dialects' (1998:11-12), and in Marett, Barwick & Ford 2013:77-78 she states that 'Emmi and Mendhe share identical sound systems and grammar' and gives joint 'Emmi-Mendhe' phoneme tables; Tryon 1974:174 calls Manda 'a dialect of Ami and Maranunggu' (86% shared cognates with Ami). The Daly Languages project page (Green & Nordlinger) confirms there is no Menthe-specific linguistic description beyond Tryon's overviews and observations in Ford's Emmi grammar. If the catalog already carries amii1238 from Ford 1998, an entry for mand1416 from the same passage is the same datum applied to the sister dialect and should be flagged as such (or the two merged at the Emmi-Menhthe level).

sources.note: Sec. 2.3.2 Word-stress p.70: each phonological word has primary stress on its initial syllable (raised pitch); every odd-numbered syllable thereafter carries secondary stress; final syllable of a polysyllable unstressed; enclitics never stressed; coverbs, incorporated nominals and bound number words keep secondary stress inside the verb complex. p.18: 'In Emmi, the initial syllable of any word carries primary stress.' pp.11-12: 'Emmi and Menhdhe are closely related dialects'. The description is of Emmi; Menhdhe (=Manda) is treated as its sister dialect, no separate Menhdhe phonology.

sources.note: No word-stress statement. States (p.77-78) 'While Emmi and Mendhe share identical sound systems and grammar, they differ slightly in lexicon and morphology' and 'Emmi and Mendhe share identical sound systems, shown in tables 3.3 and 3.4' (Emmi-Mendhe phoneme tables). This is the bridge licensing use of Ford's Emmi stress rule for Menhdhe/Manda.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. States: 'there is no specific linguistic data on Menthe other than Tryon's overviews (1968, 1974), observations in Ford's Emmi grammar (1998, 2011) and the items in Djorrk et al's (2015).. What data is available suggests that there are no significant grammatical differences, and that Menthe and Emmi are mainly distinguished on the basis of vocabulary.' Lists Green's 7 h of Menthe elicitation audio (PARADISEC IG7-001.009, speakers Jack Marrurritj, Edwin Purrel).
